# 2. Related Work

## 2.1 Dense Retrieval for Code

Code retrieval has evolved from sparse lexical methods such as BM25 \cite{robertson2009bm25} to dense neural approaches. Early pretrained code models---CodeBERT \cite{feng2020codebert}, UniXcoder \cite{guo2022unixcoder}, and InferCode \cite{bui2021infercode}---learn general-purpose code representations through masked language modeling and related pretraining objectives, enabling semantic matching beyond surface-level token overlap. More recent large-scale code models, including StarCoder2 \cite{lozhkov2024starcoder2} and Qwen2.5-Coder \cite{hui2024qwen25coder}, provide powerful encoder backbones trained on trillions of code tokens. In the retrieval domain, CodeSage \cite{zhang2024codesage} and SCodeR \cite{li2022scoder} introduce contrastive fine-tuning strategies that adapt pretrained representations for code search. The growing importance of repository-level retrieval---driven by benchmarks like SWE-bench \cite{jimenez2024swebench}---has motivated specialized systems: SweRank \cite{reddy2025swerank} formulates issue localization as code ranking, while SWE-Fixer \cite{xie2025swefixer} combines BM25 with neural reranking in a coarse-to-fine pipeline. StructFuse builds on this foundation by systematically comparing negative mining strategies---random, embedding-distance, and structure-aware---for contrastive code retrieval, demonstrating that the choice of mining strategy meaningfully affects retrieval quality.

## 2.2 Contrastive Learning for Code

Sentence-BERT \cite{reimers2019sentencebert} established contrastive fine-tuning of pretrained encoders for dense text retrieval, a paradigm that has since become dominant for code representation learning. ContraCode \cite{jain2021contracode} generates functionally equivalent program variants through compiler transformations, training models to be invariant to syntactic variation. CodeRetriever \cite{li2022coderetriever} combines unimodal code-code and bimodal code-text contrastive objectives, achieving strong results across eleven code search benchmarks. SynCoBERT \cite{wang2021syncobert} introduces syntax-guided multi-modal contrastive pretraining that aligns code, natural language, and AST modalities through identifier prediction and edge prediction objectives. ContraBERT \cite{liu2023contrabert} takes a complementary robustness-oriented approach, designing adversarial augmentation operators---including identifier renaming, dead code insertion, and operand swapping---to improve model robustness while maintaining retrieval performance. Ding et al.\ \cite{ding2022programcontrasts} use structure-guided code transformations to synthesize contrastive pairs, demonstrating that program-structure-aware augmentation improves code clone detection and vulnerability identification. GraphCodeBERT \cite{guo2021graphcodebert} incorporates data-flow edges into pretraining, demonstrating that structural information improves code understanding tasks. These methods enrich the positive pair construction space or the pretraining signal. While GraphCodeBERT uses structural edges as a pretraining objective, StructFuse addresses a complementary dimension: we systematically study how negative selection strategy---including structure-aware alternatives---affects contrastive code retrieval across encoders with distinct representation geometries.

## 2.3 Hard Negative Mining

The quality of negative examples critically affects contrastive learning \cite{chen2020simclr}. In dense text retrieval, DPR \cite{karpukhin2020dpr} established the practice of using BM25 top-ranked non-relevant passages as hard negatives. ANCE \cite{xiong2021ance} dynamically mines negatives from an approximate nearest neighbor index updated during training, while RocketQA \cite{qu2021rocketqa} introduces cross-batch denoised negatives with knowledge distillation. STAR \cite{zhan2021star} further refines this paradigm by using the retriever's own top-ranked passages as training negatives. Curriculum-based approaches---CL-DRD \cite{zeng2022cldrd} and CAPSTONE \cite{he2023capstone}---schedule negative difficulty progressively during training.

In the code domain, CoCoHaNeRe \cite{fan2025cocohanere} proposes gradient-based hard negative mining for code search, evaluating both BM25-selected and embedding-based negatives and reporting limitations of each non-differentiable strategy. However, their claim that non-differentiable embedding negatives are ineffective has not been evaluated under controlled conditions in structural code retrieval settings, where repository-level file localization involves richer structural cues than the NL$\to$code search setting studied by CoCoHaNeRe. StructFuse addresses this gap with a systematic comparison of three mining strategies---random, embedding-distance, and dataflow-aware---across decoder-only encoders with distinct representation geometries. Our results show that static embedding-distance mining provides reliable improvement at zero additional cost, establishing it as a strong baseline that requires no gradient computation or dynamic index updates. We further incorporate data-flow structure as an additional signal dimension in the comparison, grounding hardness in inter-procedural program semantics rather than embedding proximity alone.

## 2.4 Code Structure in Machine Learning

Program dependence graphs \cite{ferrante1987pdg} and code property graphs \cite{yamaguchi2014cpg} have long served program analysis; tools like CodeQL \cite{avgustinov2016ql} make inter-procedural analysis accessible at scale. In machine learning, code2vec \cite{alon2019code2vec} pioneered learning from AST paths, while ProGraML \cite{cummins2021programl} demonstrated that whole-program graph representations capturing control-flow, data-flow, and call relations are learnable and effective for compiler optimization tasks. CrossCodeEval \cite{ding2023crosscodeeval} empirically validates that cross-file context is critical for code completion, with retrieval-augmented approaches yielding clear but still far-from-ceiling improvements. RepoFusion \cite{shrivastava2023repofusion} further demonstrates that training code models to incorporate cross-file repository context via Fusion-in-Decoder significantly improves completion quality, even outperforming much larger models that lack repository awareness.

Recent inference-time graph methods bring structural reasoning to LLM-based software engineering. CodexGraph \cite{liu2025codexgraph} and RepoGraph \cite{ouyang2025repograph} build navigable code graph databases for LLM agents; LocAgent \cite{chen2025locagent} and RANGER \cite{shah2025ranger} employ multi-hop graph reasoning and MCTS-based traversal for fault localization and retrieval, respectively. GRACE \cite{wang2025grace} constructs multi-level code graphs spanning repository, module, and function granularity---integrating AST, control-flow, and data-flow edges---for hierarchical retrieval-augmented code completion. GraphCoder \cite{liu2024graphcoder} and ARISE \cite{seddik2026arise} incorporate data-flow edges---control/data dependence and definition-use chains, respectively---but their data-flow analysis remains intra-procedural in scope. Critically, these methods primarily leverage structural graphs at inference time, incurring per-query latency proportional to graph complexity. StructFuse operates in a distinct regime: we leverage inter-procedural data-flow graphs at \emph{training time} to construct an additional strategy dimension for systematic comparison, enabling analysis of how structural signals interact with encoder representation geometry---all with zero inference overhead. The two paradigms are complementary---a StructFuse-trained encoder can serve as an efficient first-stage retriever for inference-time graph systems that perform targeted reranking.

## Supplement A: Contrastive Learning for Code (insert into Section 2.2, after the ContraCode/CodeRetriever paragraph)

Beyond learning invariance to syntactic variation, contrastive pre-training has been applied to inject structural and robustness priors into code representations. SynCoBERT \cite{wang2021syncobert} introduces syntax-guided multi-modal contrastive pre-training that aligns code, natural language, and abstract syntax tree (AST) modalities through identifier prediction and AST edge prediction objectives, demonstrating that explicitly encoding syntactic structure during contrastive pre-training improves downstream code intelligence tasks. ContraBERT \cite{liu2023contrabert} takes a complementary robustness-oriented approach, designing nine data augmentation operators that generate adversarial code and comment variants---including identifier renaming, dead code insertion, and operand swapping---and further trains existing code models with contrastive objectives on these augmented pairs. ContraBERT shows that contrastive pre-training with targeted perturbations substantially improves model robustness against adversarial attacks while maintaining strong performance on standard benchmarks. These methods enrich the positive pair construction space for code contrastive learning, yet they focus on augmenting the pre-training signal rather than improving the selection of negative examples during fine-tuning. StructFuse addresses a complementary dimension: rather than improving how positive pairs are constructed, it improves which negatives the model trains against by grounding negative selection in inter-procedural data-flow structure.

## Supplement B: Hard Negative Mining in Dense Retrieval (insert into Section 2.3, after the CL-DRD sentence)

The curriculum learning paradigm for negative sampling has been further developed by CAPSTONE \cite{he2023capstone}, which addresses the training-inference discrepancy in dual-encoder dense retrieval. CAPSTONE expands documents with pseudo-queries during training and employs a curriculum sampling strategy that progressively improves the relevance between generated and real queries, effectively controlling negative difficulty through the query generation quality. This approach achieves strong results on both in-domain and out-of-domain retrieval benchmarks, reinforcing the finding that curriculum-based difficulty scheduling benefits dense retrieval training. While CAPSTONE focuses on bridging the training-inference gap through document expansion, our structure-grounded negatives provide an orthogonal form of curriculum: negatives that are hard because they do *not* share data-flow context with the positive (¬reachable_G(x,q)), not because of embedding proximity alone.

## Supplement C: Cross-File Code Understanding and Evaluation (insert into Section 2.4, before the closing paragraph, or as a new subsection bridge)

The importance of cross-file context for code understanding has been empirically validated by dedicated benchmarks. CrossCodeEval \cite{ding2023crosscodeeval} constructs a diverse, multilingual benchmark for cross-file code completion across Python, Java, TypeScript, and C\#, using static analysis to identify completion targets that strictly require cross-file dependencies. Experiments show that even state-of-the-art code LLMs struggle without cross-file context, and that retrieval-augmented approaches yield clear improvements---yet performance remains far below the ceiling, indicating substantial room for better cross-file retrieval. ProGraML \cite{cummins2021programl} provides a language-independent, graph-based program representation that captures control-flow, data-flow, and call relations across entire programs, achieving strong results on data-flow analysis tasks. ProGraML demonstrates that whole-program structural representations are learnable and informative, providing conceptual grounding for StructFuse's use of inter-procedural data-flow graphs as a training signal. Together, these resources underscore that cross-file structural dependencies and realistic query distributions are critical dimensions for advancing code retrieval---precisely the dimensions that StructFuse's structure-grounded training targets.
